title: Three perfect days in San Francisco, before the holidays
dek: Ballet with the Symphony, burritos and murals in the Mission, and Egyptian gold in Golden Gate Park: a pre-Thanksgiving weekend that keeps you warm and mostly dry.

hero.caption: Mission Dolores Park, where Saturday's walk looks out over the Mission toward downtown.

intro:
This is the last weekend before Thanksgiving, and San Francisco is starting to turn toward the holidays without quite getting there. The ice rink in Union Square opened on November 4, but the city-funded Christmas tree beside it is not due to be lit until around Black Friday. The Great Dickens Christmas Fair opens its five-weekend run at the Cow Palace on Saturday, and the city's museums are full: SFMOMA is in the last ten days of its Graciela Iturbide retrospective, and the de Young has 130 objects from Cairo's Egyptian Museum and the Luxor Museum in *Treasures of the Pharaohs*.

The other big night is musical. On Friday and Saturday the San Francisco Symphony shares the Davies Symphony Hall stage with Alonzo King LINES Ballet, with James Gaffigan conducting Copland's *Appalachian Spring* and Debussy's *Prelude to the Afternoon of a Faun*. On Sunday afternoon the Warriors host the Celtics at Chase Center, and on Saturday night the Jonas Brothers play the same arena, so Mission Bay will be busy both evenings.

The weather needs watching. On Monday the National Weather Service expected Friday's rain to taper off during the day, a new system to bring more from Saturday, and highs 5 to 10 degrees below normal. So the plan leans indoors where it can. Friday covers SoMa and the Civic Center: coffee at a roastery, a long morning at SFMOMA, a City Hall tour, roast chicken at Zuni and the ballet. Saturday stays in the Mission, from Tartine and the old mission to El Farolito, the murals of Balmy Alley, dinner at Foreign Cinema and a nightcap at Trick Dog. Sunday is Golden Gate Park and the Inner Sunset: the de Young, San Tung's chicken wings, the Conservatory of Flowers, then a walk up the Panhandle to dinner at Nopa. Book the Symphony, Zuni and Foreign Cinema now, and pack a rain shell.

days.title: Friday: SoMa, the Civic Center and the ballet
days.intro: A day of big rooms: a roastery, a seven-floor museum, a Beaux-Arts rotunda and a concert hall, all a short walk or one Muni ride apart.

stops.name: Sightglass Coffee
stops.text: Start at the original Sightglass on 7th Street, the company's flagship, which is roastery, coffee bar and headquarters under one high wooden roof. You can watch the roasting and the barista training from the bar while you drink, and the company runs public tastings on Fridays. Order a pour-over or a cortado and something from the pastry case, and take a seat by the windows. Practical note: it opens at 6:30 a.m. on weekdays and closes at 5 p.m.; SFMOMA is about a 15-minute walk east.

stops.name: SFMOMA: Graciela Iturbide
stops.text: Give San Francisco's modern art museum the whole morning. *Graciela Iturbide: Between Two Worlds*, on the third floor, is a major retrospective of the Mexican photographer's black-and-white work, and it closes on November 29, so this is one of its last weekends. Then go up through the newly rehung Fisher Collection galleries and Rose B. Simpson's sculpture show *Behold*. Practical note: the museum is open 10 a.m. to 5 p.m. on Fridays and closed on Wednesdays. Book timed tickets online; construction work affects the atrium and some upper floors, so check access on the day.
stops.wiki: San Francisco Museum of Modern Art

stops.name: Saigon Sandwich
stops.text: Take Muni or a 20-minute walk across Market Street to this tiny counter on Larkin, which has been making some of the city's best-loved bánh mì for decades. The Infatuation puts it in its 2026 list of the city's 25 essential restaurants, recommending the roast chicken or roast pork. The bread is crusty, the pickled vegetables sharp, and lunch costs very little. Practical note: there is barely room to stand, so take your sandwich to the Civic Center plaza or eat it on the City Hall steps. It opens daily from about 7 a.m.

stops.name: San Francisco City Hall
stops.text: City Hall's dome is taller than the U.S. Capitol's, and the marble rotunda and grand staircase underneath are one of the best free rooms in town. Volunteer docents lead free tours on Fridays at 11 a.m. and 1 p.m., about 45 minutes to an hour, covering the building's history and architecture. Practical note: sign up at the Docent Tour kiosk in the Goodlett Place elevator lobby; the building is open to the public on weekdays from 8 a.m. to 6 p.m. and you will pass through security.

stops.name: Zuni Café
stops.text: Zuni has been on this triangular corner of Market Street since 1979, and its wood-fired roast chicken for two, served on bread salad, is still the dish people come back for. It takes about an hour, so order it as soon as you sit, with the Caesar salad and a few oysters to fill the wait; finish with the espresso granita. The long copper bar and the tall windows onto passing Muni trains are half the pleasure. Practical note: book through OpenTable, which takes reservations up to 60 days ahead. Davies Symphony Hall is a five-minute walk.

stops.name: Alonzo King LINES Ballet with the San Francisco Symphony
stops.text: San Francisco's own contemporary ballet company joins the orchestra for three nights, with James Gaffigan conducting. Dancers perform to Debussy's *Prelude to the Afternoon of a Faun* and the suite from Copland's *Appalachian Spring*, and the program also includes Prokofiev's *Sinfonia concertante*, with the Symphony's principal cellist Rainer Eudeikis as soloist. Alonzo King's choreography is long-limbed and very musical, and seeing it with a full orchestra rather than a recording is a rare treat. Practical note: performances are Thursday to Saturday at 7:30 p.m.; buy tickets from the Symphony's site.

days.title: Saturday: the Mission, from the old mission to Trick Dog
days.intro: A day on foot in one neighborhood: the city's oldest building, its best-known burrito, its murals and two of its longest-running places to eat and drink.

stops.name: Tartine Bakery
stops.text: Elisabeth Prueitt and Chad Robertson's corner bakery at Guerrero and 18th is where much of the city's bread and pastry obsession started. Get here early, before the line reaches the corner, for a morning bun, a croissant and a coffee,. Practical note: it is open daily from 7:30 a.m. to 6 p.m. (closed only on Thanksgiving and Christmas). Seats are for customers who have ordered and paid, and you can order ahead online. Mission Dolores is a five-minute walk.

stops.name: Mission Dolores
stops.text: Founded in 1776, Mission San Francisco de Asís gave the neighborhood its name, and its small whitewashed chapel is the oldest intact building in the city. Look up at the painted ceiling, then walk through to the cemetery and garden, where about 5,000 Ohlone, Miwok and other First Californians are buried alongside early settlers, and the Ohlone plant garden. The tall basilica next door is from the 20th century. Practical note: the mission opens at 10 a.m. on weekends (until 5 p.m.) for self-guided visits, no reservation needed. It is also the best rain shelter of the morning.

stops.name: Mission Dolores Park
stops.text: Two blocks south, climb to the top of Dolores Park's southwest corner, near 20th and Church, for the view that ends up on postcards: palm trees, the Mission's rooftops and the downtown towers behind. If the weather holds, walk east along 20th Street through the Mission's quieter blocks of Victorians; if it doesn't, keep this short. Practical note: from 11 a.m. to 4 p.m. the free Sábado Gigante festival of Native arts and culture fills the 16th Street BART plaza, a ten-minute detour, before you head south on Mission Street to lunch.

stops.name: Taqueria El Farolito
stops.text: The argument over the city's best burrito usually ends at El Farolito, and The Infatuation's 2026 list of essential San Francisco restaurants sides with it. Order the super burrito with carne asada, or a super quesadilla suiza with al pastor, and grab a horchata. It is fluorescent-lit, loud and fast, which is the point. Practical note: the line moves quickly; tables turn over fast, and a super burrito is easily enough for two light eaters. It sits right by the 24th Street BART station.

stops.name: Balmy Alley and 24th Street
stops.text: Walk east along 24th Street, the heart of the Calle 24 Latino Cultural District, past panaderías, botanicas and fruit stands, to Balmy Alley between 24th and 25th. Its garage doors and fences carry murals painted since the 1970s, many about Central America, immigration and the neighborhood's own fights over rent and displacement; the paintings change as artists repaint them. Practical note: allow an hour, and stop for a pan dulce on the way back. If Saturday's rain arrives early, cut this short and keep the afternoon for a rest before dinner.

stops.name: Foreign Cinema
stops.text: Behind an unmarked passage on Mission Street, Foreign Cinema has served California cooking in a courtyard where films are projected on a wall since 1999. Gayle Pirie's menu changes with the market, so start with oysters or crudo and follow the seasons from there; diners this month have praised the duck and the seafood risotto. Practical note: dinner runs 5 to 10 p.m. on Saturday; book on OpenTable and ask for the heated courtyard if you want the films, or the indoor dining room if it is raining.

stops.name: Trick Dog
stops.text: Trick Dog has been one of the country's most admired cocktail bars, and it reinvents its menu around a theme every so often. The current one, *Meet Me in the City*, is a hardbound book of San Francisco portraits by local photographers, with 16 drinks inspired by the pictures: try the Dolores, a fizzy white Negroni with green tea, or International Orange, a whiskey drink named for the Golden Gate Bridge. Practical note: cocktails are $18; it is a 10-minute walk from Foreign Cinema.

days.title: Sunday: Golden Gate Park and the Inner Sunset
days.intro: A day for rain or shine: Egyptian treasures, a glasshouse of tropical plants and a walk through the park to one of the city's best dining rooms.

stops.name: Arizmendi Bakery
stops.text: This worker-owned cooperative bakery on Ninth Avenue celebrated 25 years in October 2025, and the neighborhood still lines up for its cheese rolls, focaccia and the pizza of the day. Get a coffee, a cheese roll and a slice of whatever bread came out last, and eat on the bench outside or take it into the park. Practical note: it opens at 7:30 a.m. Tuesday to Sunday. The N Judah stops a block away, and the de Young is a ten-minute walk north through the park's Music Concourse.

stops.name: de Young Museum: Treasures of the Pharaohs
stops.text: *Treasures of the Pharaohs* brings 130 objects on loan from Cairo's Egyptian Museum and the Luxor Museum, among them the gilded outer coffin of Thuya, a gold and lapis pendant of Amenemope and a chair made for Princess Sitamun, plus finds from the recently excavated Golden City near Luxor. Afterwards ride up the copper-clad Hamon Observation Tower, which is free, for a view over the park to the Pacific. Practical note: the museum opens at 9:30 a.m. Tuesday to Sunday; the show needs a special exhibition ticket, so book a morning slot online.

stops.name: San Tung
stops.text: Walk back south to Irving Street for San Tung's dry-fried chicken wings, sticky, crisp and coated in a sweet garlic glaze; Axios San Francisco called them the best thing its reporter ate this spring. Add a plate of dumplings to round out lunch. Practical note: expect a line at lunchtime, so put your name down and wander Irving Street while you wait. San Tung is closed Tuesdays and Wednesdays and its hours vary, so check before you go.

stops.name: Conservatory of Flowers
stops.text: The white wood-and-glass Conservatory of Flowers, built in 1879, is the oldest building in Golden Gate Park and the warmest place in it on a cold November afternoon. Inside are rooms of lowland and highland tropical plants, giant water lilies and orchids, and the humid air is welcome after a wet walk. Practical note: it is open 10 a.m. to 4:30 p.m. (last entry 4 p.m.) and closed on Wednesdays. If you are back this way after dark, *Photosynthesis*, a free light show on the building, starts half an hour after sunset.

stops.name: The Panhandle
stops.text: Leave the park by its eastern end and walk the Panhandle, the narrow strip of eucalyptus and lawns that runs eight blocks toward Divisadero Street. It is where the city jogs, cycles and walks its dogs, and the grand Victorians lining Fell and Oak streets are a quick lesson in the city's architecture. Practical note: it takes about 25 minutes at an easy pace, on a paved path, and ends a block from dinner at Nopa. If the rain is heavy, take the 5 Fulton bus instead.

stops.name: Nopa
stops.text: Nopa opened in a former bank on Divisadero in 2006 and helped turn the street into a dining destination; twenty years on, the San Francisco Standard calls it an institution. The menu changes daily with what comes from Bay Area farms, and the wood-fired oven runs all night, so order the flatbread, whatever the kitchen is roasting, and the burger if you want something hearty. Practical note: Sunday dinner runs 5 to 9:30 p.m.; book on Nopa's website, or arrive after 5:30 p.m. and give your name to the host for a seat at the bar.

stay.name: The St. Regis San Francisco
stay.text: The St. Regis sits in a tower on Third Street right beside SFMOMA, with the Museum of the African Diaspora at its base, so Friday's museum morning starts at your door. The hotel has a spa and collected a long list of 2026 Hotelier's Choice awards, including for its views. Davies Symphony Hall is a short taxi ride away.

stay.name: Palace Hotel
stay.text: The Palace turned 150 in 2025. Rebuilt after the 1906 earthquake, it has the Garden Court, with about 80,000 panes of stained glass overhead, the wood-paneled Pied Piper Bar with its Maxfield Parrish painting, and a small museum of its history. The green goddess salad was created here in 1923. It is on Market Street, a step from BART and Muni for every day of this plan.

stay.name: Hayes Valley Inn
stay.text: A simple, inexpensive inn on a quiet block of Hayes Valley, with a shared kitchen and plain rooms, and recommended in 2025 as one of the city's best affordable stays. Its location suits this weekend: Zuni and Davies Symphony Hall are a few minutes' walk away, and Muni's underground trains at Van Ness take you toward the Mission and the Inner Sunset. Read the room descriptions carefully before you book.

events.name: Alonzo King LINES Ballet & Appalachian Spring
events.when: Thu. to Sat., Nov. 19 to 21, 7:30 p.m.
events.where: Davies Symphony Hall, 201 Van Ness Ave.
events.text: The San Francisco Symphony and James Gaffigan accompany LINES Ballet in Debussy and Copland, with Prokofiev's Sinfonia concertante on the same program.

events.name: In Their Name: Día de Los Muertos 2026 (closing)
events.when: Fri. noon to 7 p.m.; closing party 6 to 9 p.m.
events.text: The last day of SOMArts' 27th annual Day of the Dead exhibition of altars and installations, free to visit; the closing reception and drag show costs $15.

events.name: Great Dickens Christmas Fair (opening weekend)
events.when: Sat. and Sun., 10 a.m. to 6 p.m.
events.text: The halls of the Cow Palace become Victorian London, with theaters, pubs, dance parties and Dickens characters, for five weekends to December 20.

events.name: Sábado Gigante: Native arts and culture festival
events.text: A free afternoon of Native arts and culture on the plaza at 16th and Mission, a short walk from Saturday's stops.

events.name: Jonas Brothers
events.text: The brothers bring their arena tour to San Francisco; expect busy T Third trains and traffic around Mission Bay.

events.name: The Music Man
events.when: Fri. 7:30 p.m.; weekend matinees and evenings
events.text: The touring production of Meredith Willson's musical plays the Orpheum through the weekend, a few blocks from the Civic Center.

events.name: Warriors vs. Boston Celtics
events.text: An old rivalry at home; the first 10,000 fans get a Philadelphia Warriors championship pennant, marking the franchise's Philadelphia years.

know: From SFO, BART runs straight to Civic Center, Powell Street and the 16th and 24th Street stations in the Mission in about half an hour; a taxi or rideshare to downtown takes 25 to 40 minutes. From Oakland, take the BART airport connector and change for San Francisco.

A Clipper card, or Clipper in your phone's wallet, works on BART, Muni buses and the underground Muni trains. The N Judah runs from downtown to the Inner Sunset for Sunday, and the 5 Fulton runs along the park's north side.
Tip 18 to 22 percent at sit-down restaurants. Many San Francisco bills add a surcharge for staff health care; it is not a tip.
Rain is likely on Friday morning and again from Saturday, with highs 5 to 10 degrees below normal. Pack a rain shell and a warm layer, and keep the outdoor walks flexible.

Watch the day-of-week hours: SFMOMA is closed on Wednesdays, the de Young on Mondays, the Conservatory of Flowers on Wednesdays, and City Hall's free docent tours run only on weekdays, with Friday tours at 11 a.m. and 1 p.m.
Mission Bay will be crowded on Saturday night (Jonas Brothers) and Sunday evening (Warriors vs. Celtics) at Chase Center; allow extra time on the T Third and around the arena.
Thanksgiving is Thursday, November 26. Many restaurants close that day, Tartine included. The Union Square ice rink is open, but the tree there is not expected to be lit until around Black Friday.
